newsitem.title: USA: USDA seen raising '97/98 soy end stocks forecast.
newsitem.headline: USDA seen raising '97/98 soy end stocks forecast.

text.p: The largest soybean acreage planted in the U.S. since 1982 should ensure that the U.S. Department of Agriculture raises its estimate for 1997/98 (Sept/Aug) ending stocks later this week, analysts said.
And less-than-expected corn plantings will lead to a cut in USDA's 1997/98 (Sept/Aug) corn ending stocks forecast although supplies remain plentiful, they added.
"We've another 6.7 million acres (of soybeans versus last year). It is tough to run away from that," said analyst Jerry Gidel of Dean Witter.
USDA is due to revise its U.S. supply and demand estimates on Friday at 0730 CDT/1230 GMT.
"We can have all the demand in the world (for soybeans) but you can't use it all," Gidel said.
Last week the USDA put this year's soybean plantings at 70.9 million acres, up from a previous projection of 68.8 million and sharply above last year's 64.2 million.
Gidel said he expected USDA's 1997/98 soybean ending stocks estimate to be raised to between 280 million and 300 million bushels, versus a previous estimate of 240 million.

Analysts said the strength of soybean prices, with the nearby contract on the Chicago Board of Trade in May rising above $9.00 a bushel for the first time since August 1988, had encouraged heavy plantings.

Soybean ending stocks for 1996/97 are expected to remain around USDA's current estimate of 130 million, with a possible reduction in the export total offset by an possible increase in the projection for domestic crushings.
Analysts said they expected USDA's 1996/97 corn ending stocks estimate to be either unchanged or slightly above its current projection of 909 million bushels.
FIMAT analyst Dan Cekander said USDA could cut its projection for 1996/97 exports and therefore raise ending stocks by 25 million bushels.
And Gidel of Dean Witter said the food, seed and industrial use total (which includes ethanol) could be cut by 20 million bringing ending stocks up to 929 million bushels.
Corn ending stocks for 1997/98 should, however, be cut from USDA's current projection of 1.349 billion bushels due to lower than expected plantings.
Last week USDA put planted area at 80.2 million acres, down from its previous estimate of 81.4 million although still above last year's area of 79.5 million.
Gidel, of Dean Witter, said USDA might cut the corn estimate by 100 million bushels to 1.25 billion but even at that level, stocks were be adequate.
"To get this thing (the market) exciting, you need one billion or less," he said.

Wheat ending stocks for 1997/98 (June/May) were expected to be raised to between 600 million and 700 million bushels, up from USDA's current projection for 579 million as prospects for this year's winter wheat crop continue to improve, analysts said.
"That is the range the market is in today (600 to 700 million bushels)," said Cargill Investor Services analyst Warren King, noting the total would be the highest since 1990/91.
